The '''square root of 5''', denoted {{tmath|\sqrt5}}, is the positive [[real number]] that, when multiplied by itself, gives the natural number [[5 (number)|5]]. Along with its [[Conjugate (square roots)|conjugate]] {{tmath|-\sqrt5}}, it solves the [[quadratic equation]] {{tmath|1= x^2 - 5 = 0}}, making it a [[quadratic integer]], a type of [[algebraic number]]. {{tmath|\sqrt5}} is an [[irrational number]], meaning it cannot be written as a fraction of [[integer]]s.<ref>[[Joseph Dauben|Dauben, Joseph W.]] (June 1983) [[Scientific American]] ''Georg Cantor and the origins of transfinite set theory.'' Volume 248; Page 122.</ref> The first thirty<!-- Consistent with [[Square root of 2]] and [[e (mathematical constant)]] --> significant digits of its [[decimal expansion]] are:<ref>{{Cite OEIS|sequencenumber=A002163|name=Decimal expansion of square root of 5}}</ref>

{{block indent|{{gaps|2.23606|79774|99789|69640|91736|6873...}}}}

A length of {{tmath|\sqrt5}} can be constructed as the [[diagonal]] of a {{tmath|2 \times 1}} unit [[rectangle]]. {{tmath|\sqrt5}} also appears throughout in the metrical geometry of shapes with fivefold symmetry; the ratio between diagonal and side of a [[regular pentagon]] is the [[golden ratio]] {{tmath|1= \varphi = \tfrac12\bigl(1 + \sqrt5~\!\bigr)}}.

==Rational approximations==
{{See also|Square root algorithms}}
The square root of 5 is an [[irrational number]], meaning it can not be exactly represented as a fraction {{tmath|x/y}} where {{tmath|x}} and {{tmath|y}} are [[integer]]s. However, it can be approximated arbitrarily closely by such [[rational number]]s.

Particularly good approximations are the integer solutions of [[Pell's equation]]s,
:<math>x^2 - 5y^2 = 1 \quad \text{and} \quad x^2 - 5y^2 = -1,</math>
which can be algebraically rearranged into the form
:<math>\frac{x}{y} = \sqrt{5 \pm \frac{1}{y^2}} .</math>

For example, the approximation {{tmath|1=\textstyle 2 = \sqrt{5 - 1 } }}, which is accurate to about 10%, satisfies the negative Pell's equation, {{tmath|1=\textstyle 2^2 - 5\cdot 1^2 = 4 - 5 = -1}}; likewise, the approximation {{tmath|1=\textstyle \tfrac94 = \sqrt{5 + \tfrac{1}{16} }  = 2.25 }}, which is accurate within 1%, satisfies the positive equation, {{tmath|1=\textstyle 9^2 - 5\cdot 4^2 = 81 - 80 = 1}}. These two approximations are the respective fundamental solutions of each Pell's equation, to which [[Pell's equation#Additional solutions from the fundamental solution|additional solutions are algebraically related]].

Solutions to both Pell's equations can also be found systematically by following the [[Euclidean algorithm#Rational and real numbers|Euclidean algorithm]], resulting in the [[simple continued fraction]] for {{tmath|\sqrt5}},<ref>{{OEIS|id=A040002}}</ref>

:<math> \sqrt5 = [2; 4, 4, 4, \ldots{}] = 2 + \cfrac 1 {4 + \cfrac 1 {4 + \cfrac 1 {4 + {{\vphantom x} \atop \displaystyle\ddots}}}}. </math>

Each step {{tmath|n}} of the algorithm produces a better approximation {{tmath|x_n / y_n}}, one of the [[convergent (continued fraction)|convergents]] (partial evaluations) of this continued fraction. These are a sequence of [[Simple continued fraction#Best rational approximations|best rational approximation]]s to {{tmath|\sqrt5}}, each more accurate than any other rational approximation with the same or smaller denominator. They give all of the solutions to Pell's equations, satisfying {{tmath|1=\textstyle x_n^2 - 5y_n^2 = (-1)^n}}.<ref name=conrad>{{cite web |last1=Conrad |first1=Keith |title=Pell's Equation II |url=https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/ugradnumthy/pelleqn2.pdf |website=uconn.edu |access-date=17 March 2022 }}</ref> The first several convergents to the continued fraction are:<ref>Their numerators are 2, 9, 38, 161, ... {{OEIS|id=A001077}}. {{pb}} Their denominators are 1, 4, 17, 72, ... {{OEIS|id=A001076}}.</ref>

{{Table alignment}}

In the [[Limit of a sequence|limit]], these approximations converge to {{tmath|\sqrt5}}. That is, {{tmath|1=\textstyle \lim_{n\to\infty} x_n/y_n = \sqrt5}}.

One of the oldest methods of calculating a square root of a number {{tmath|d}}, the [[Babylonian method]],<ref>The Babylonian method is also called ''Heron's method'', as it appeared in [[Heron of Alexandria|Heron]]'s ''Metrica'', in roughly the modern form. The earlier Babylonian approach was equivalent but more cumbersome. See {{citation |last1=Fowler |first1=David |author1-link=David Fowler (mathematician)|last2=Robson |first2=Eleanor |author2-link=Eleanor Robson |year=1998 |title=Square Root Approximations in Old Babylonian Mathematics: YBC 7289 in Context |journal=Historia Mathematica |volume=25 |pages=366–378 |doi=10.1006/hmat.1998.2209 |doi-access=free }}</ref> starts with an initial guess {{tmath|x_0}}, and at each step finds a new approximation by averaging the previous approximation and {{tmath|d}} times its [[multiplicative inverse|reciprocal]], {{tmath|1= x_{n+1} = \tfrac12(x_n + d/x_n)}}. This is the special case, for the function {{tmath|1=\textstyle f(x) = x^2 - d}}, of [[Newton's method]] for finding the root of an arbitrary function. For a typical guess, the approximation [[Quadratic convergence|converges quadratically]] (roughly doubles the number of correct digits at each step).<ref>{{citation |last=Parris |first=Richard |title=The Root-Finding Route to Chaos |journal=The College Mathematics Journal |year=1991 |volume=22 |number=1 |pages=48–55 |jstor=2686739 }}</ref>

The initial guess is somewhat arbitrary, but when approximating {{tmath|\sqrt5}} by this method, usually {{tmath|1= x_0 = 2}} is chosen.<ref>{{citation |last=Motzer |first=Renate |year=2001 |title=Fractions, Ratios, and Roots, |publisher=Springer |place=Wiesbaden |chapter=Irrational Numbers |at=Ch. 8, {{pgs|35–39}} |doi=10.1007/978-3-658-32574-9_8 |isbn=978-3-658-32573-2}}</ref> With this choice, the {{tmath|n}}th approximation is equal to the {{tmath|2^n}}th convergent of the continued fraction for {{tmath|\sqrt5}}.<ref>{{OEIS|id=A081459}}, {{OEIS|id=A081460}}</ref>

:<math>\begin{align}
x_0 &= \frac{2}{1} & \!\!x_1 &= \frac{9}{4} & \!\!x_2 & = \frac{161}{72} & \!\!x_3 &= \frac{51841}{23184} \\[3mu]
&=2.{\color{BrickRed} 0}, & &=2.2{\color{BrickRed} 5}, & &\approx 2.236{\color{BrickRed} 1}, & &\approx 2.23606\,7977{\color{BrickRed} 9}, & \!\! \ldots,
\end{align}</math>
with digits that differ from the decimal expansion of {{tmath|\sqrt5}} highlighted in red.

==Relation to the golden ratio and Fibonacci numbers==
{{also| Golden field}}
[[File:Golden Rectangle Construction.svg|thumb|The {{math|{{sfrac|1|2}}√5}} diagonal of a half [[square]] forms the basis for the geometrical construction of a [[golden rectangle]].]]
The [[golden ratio]] {{tmath|\varphi}} is the [[arithmetic mean]] of 1 and <math>\sqrt{5}</math>.<ref>Browne, Malcolm W. (July 30, 1985) [[New York Times]] ''Puzzling Crystals Plunge Scientists into Uncertainty.'' Section: C; Page 1. (Note: this is a widely cited article).</ref> <math>\sqrt{5}</math> has a relationship to the golden ratio and [[golden ratio#Golden ratio conjugate and powers|its algebraic conjugate]] {{tmath|\overline\varphi}} as is expressed in the following formulae:

<math display=block>
\begin{align}
\sqrt{5} &= \varphi - \overline\varphi = 2\varphi - 1 = 1 - 2\overline\varphi, \\[5pt]
\varphi &= \frac{1 + \sqrt{5}}{2} = \overline\varphi + \sqrt5 = - \frac{1}{~\!\overline\varphi\!~} = 1 - \overline\varphi, \\[5pt]
\overline\varphi &= \frac{1 - \sqrt{5}}{2} = \varphi - \sqrt5 = - \frac{1}{\varphi} = 1 - \varphi.
\end{align}
</math>
<math>\sqrt{5}</math>  then figures in the closed form expression for the [[Fibonacci number]]s:<ref>{{citation|title=Proofs that Really Count: The Art of Combinatorial Proof|title-link=Proofs That Really Count|volume=27|series=Dolciani Mathematical Expositions|first1=Arthur T.|last1=Benjamin|first2=Jennifer J.|last2=Quinn|author2-link=Jennifer Quinn|publisher=American Mathematical Society|year=2022|isbn=9781470472597|page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=MR6bEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA137 137]}}</ref>

<math display=block>F(n) = \frac{\varphi^n-\overline\varphi^n}{\sqrt 5}.</math>

The quotient {{tmath|\sqrt{5}\big/\varphi}} provides an interesting pattern of continued fractions and are related to the ratios between the Fibonacci numbers and the [[Lucas number]]s:<ref>[[Richard K. Guy]]: "The Strong Law of Small Numbers". ''[[American Mathematical Monthly]]'', vol. 95, 1988, pp. 675–712</ref>

<math display=block>\begin{align}
\frac{\sqrt{5}}{\varphi} = \frac{5 - \sqrt{5}}{2} & = 1.381966\dots = [1; 2, 1, 1, 1, \ldots]
\end{align}</math>

The convergents feature the Lucas numbers as numerators and the Fibonacci numbers as denominators:

<math display=block>
\frac{1}{1}, \frac{3}{2}, \frac{4}{3}, \frac{7}{5}, \frac{11}{8}, \frac{18}{13}, \frac{29}{21}, \ldots, \frac{L_{n}}{F_{n+1}}, \ldots
</math>

In the [[limit of a sequence|limit]],
<math display=block>
\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{F_{n+1}}{F_n} = \frac{L_{n+1}}{L_n} = \varphi, \qquad
\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{L_n}{F_n} = \sqrt{5}.
</math>

More precisely, the convergents to the continued fraction for {{tmath|\sqrt5}} (see {{slink||Rational approximations}} above) are:
:<math>\frac{2}{1}, \frac{9}{4}, \frac{38}{17}, \frac{161}{72}, \frac{682}{305}, \ldots, \frac{\tfrac12L_{3n}}{\tfrac12F_{3n}}, \ldots.</math>

==Geometry==
[[File:pinwheel 1.svg|250px|thumb|right|Decomposition of a {{math|1{{thinsp}}×{{thinsp}}2}} right triangle into five similar triangles, the basis for the aperiodic [[pinwheel tiling]]]]
[[File:Root rectangles Hambidge 1920.png|250px|thumb|right|[[Jay Hambidge]]'s construction of "root rectangles"]]
[[File:distances_between_double_cube_corners.svg|thumb|right|Distances between vertices of a double [[unit cube]] are square roots of the first six [[natural number]]s. ({{math|√7}} is not possible due to [[Legendre's three-square theorem]].)]]

[[Geometry|Geometrically]], <math>\sqrt{5}</math> corresponds to the [[diagonal]] of a rectangle whose sides are of length [[1 (number)|1]] and [[2 (number)|2]], as is evident from the [[Pythagorean theorem]]. Such a rectangle can be obtained by halving a square, or by placing two equal squares side by side. This can be used to subdivide a square grid into a tilted square grid with five times as many squares, forming the basis for a [[subdivision surface]].<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Ivrissimtzis | first1 = Ioannis P.
 | last2 = Dodgson | first2 = Neil A.
 | last3 = Sabin | first3 = Malcolm
 | editor1-last = Dodgson | editor1-first = Neil A.
 | editor2-last = Floater | editor2-first = Michael S.
 | editor3-last = Sabin | editor3-first = Malcolm A.
 | contribution = <math>\sqrt5</math>-subdivision
 | doi = 10.1007/3-540-26808-1_16
 | location = Berlin
 | mr = 2112357
 | pages = 285–299
 | publisher = Springer
 | series = Mathematics and Visualization
 | title = Advances in multiresolution for geometric modelling: Papers from the workshop (MINGLE 2003) held in Cambridge, September 9–11, 2003
 | year = 2005| isbn = 3-540-21462-3
 }}</ref> Together with the algebraic relationship between <math>\sqrt{5}</math> and {{tmath|\varphi}}, this forms the basis for the geometrical construction of a [[golden rectangle]] from a square, and for the construction of a [[regular polygon|regular]] [[pentagon]] given its side (since the side-to-diagonal ratio in a regular pentagon is {{tmath|\varphi}}).

Since two adjacent faces of a [[cube]] would unfold into a {{tmath|1\mathbin{:}2}} rectangle, the ratio between the length of the cube's [[edge (geometry)|edge]] and the shortest distance from one of its [[vertex (geometry)|vertices]] to the opposite one, when traversing the cube ''surface'', is <math>\sqrt{5}</math>. By contrast, the shortest distance when traversing through the ''inside'' of the cube corresponds to the length of the cube diagonal, which is the [[square root of three]] times the edge.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Sutton |first=David |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vgo7bTxDmIsC&pg=PA55 |title=Platonic & Archimedean Solids |publisher=Walker & Company |year=2002 |isbn=0802713866 |pages=55 |language=en}}</ref>

A rectangle with side proportions <math>1\mathbin{:}\sqrt{5}</math> is part of the series of [[dynamic rectangle]]s, which are based on proportions {{tmath|\sqrt1}}, {{tmath|\sqrt2}}, {{tmath|\sqrt3}}, {{tmath|\sqrt4}}, {{tmath|\sqrt5}}, ... and successively constructed using the diagonal of the previous root rectangle, starting from a square.<ref>{{Citation | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=1KI0JVuWYGkC&q=intitle:%22Geometry+of+Design%22+%22root+5%22&pg=PA41 | author = Kimberly Elam | title = Geometry of Design: Studies in Proportion and Composition | place = New York | publisher = Princeton Architectural Press | year = 2001 | isbn = 1-56898-249-6 }}</ref> A root-5 rectangle is particularly notable in that it can be split into a square and two equal golden rectangles or into two golden rectangles of different sizes.<ref>{{Citation | title = The Elements of Dynamic Symmetry | author = Jay Hambidge | publisher = Courier Dover Publications | year = 1967 | isbn = 0-486-21776-0 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=VYJK2F-dh2oC&q=%22root+five+rectangle%22++section+inauthor:hambidge&pg=PA26 }}</ref> It can also be decomposed as the union of two equal golden rectangles whose intersection forms a square. These shapes pictorially represent the algebraic relationships between <math>\sqrt{5}</math>, {{tmath|\varphi}} and {{tmath|\varphi^{-1} }} mentioned above.

==Trigonometry==
The square root of 5 appears in [[exact trigonometric constants|trigonometric constants]] related to the angles in a regular pentagon and decagon, which when combined which can be combined with other angles involving <math>\sqrt{2}</math> and <math>\sqrt{3}</math> to describe [[sine and cosine|sines and cosines]] of every [[angle]] whose measure in [[degree (angle)|degrees]] is [[divisible]] by 3 but not by 15.<ref>[http://www.jdawiseman.com/papers/easymath/surds_sin_cos.html Julian D. A. Wiseman, "Sin and cos in surds"]</ref> The simplest of these are
:<math>\begin{align}
\sin\frac{\pi}{10} = \sin 18^\circ &= \tfrac{1}{4}(\sqrt5-1) = \frac{1}{\sqrt5+1}, \\[5pt]
\sin\frac{\pi}{5} = \sin 36^\circ &= \tfrac{1}{4}\sqrt{2(5-\sqrt5)}, \\[5pt]
\sin\frac{3\pi}{10} = \sin 54^\circ &= \tfrac{1}{4}(\sqrt5+1) = \frac{1}{\sqrt5-1}, \\[5pt]
\sin\frac{2\pi}{5} = \sin 72^\circ &= \tfrac{1}{4}\sqrt{2(5+\sqrt5)}\, . \end{align}</math>

Computing its value was therefore historically important for generating [[trigonometric tables]]. Since <math>\sqrt{5}</math> is geometrically linked to half-square rectangles and to pentagons, it also appears frequently in formulae for the geometric properties of figures derived from them, such as in the formula for the volume of a [[dodecahedron]].<ref name=":0" />

==Diophantine approximations==
[[Hurwitz's theorem (number theory)|Hurwitz's theorem]] in [[Diophantine approximations]] states that every [[irrational number]] {{math|''x''}} can be approximated by [[infinite set|infinitely many]] [[rational number]]s {{math|{{sfrac|''m''|''n''}}}} in [[lowest terms]] in such a way that
:<math> \left|x - \frac{m}{n}\right| < \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}\,n^2} </math>
and that <math>\sqrt{5}</math> is best possible, in the sense that for any larger constant than <math>\sqrt{5}</math>, there are some irrational numbers {{math|''x''}} for which only finitely many such approximations exist.<ref>{{Citation | last1=LeVeque | first1=William Judson | title=Topics in number theory | publisher=Addison-Wesley Publishing Co., Inc., Reading, Mass. |mr=0080682 | year=1956}}</ref>

Closely related to this is the theorem<ref name=khinchin/> that of any three consecutive [[convergent (continued fraction)|convergent]]s {{math|{{sfrac|''p''<sub>''i''</sub>|''q''<sub>''i''</sub>}}}}, {{math|{{sfrac|''p''<sub>''i''+1</sub>|''q''<sub>''i''+1</sub>}}}}, {{math|{{sfrac|''p''<sub>''i''+2</sub>|''q''<sub>''i''+2</sub>}}}}, of a number {{math|''α''}}, at least one of the three inequalities holds:
:<math>\left|\alpha - {p_i\over q_i}\right| < {1\over \sqrt5 q_i^2}, \quad
\left|\alpha - {p_{i+1}\over q_{i+1}}\right| < {1\over \sqrt5 q_{i+1}^2}, \quad
\left|\alpha - {p_{i+2}\over q_{i+2}}\right| < {1\over \sqrt5 q_{i+2}^2}.</math>

And the <math>\sqrt{5}</math> in the denominator is the best bound possible since the convergents of the golden ratio make the difference on the left-hand side arbitrarily close to the value on the right-hand side.  In particular, one cannot obtain a tighter bound by considering sequences of four or more consecutive convergents.<ref name=khinchin>{{Citation | last1=Khinchin | author-link=A. Ya. Khinchin | first1=Aleksandr Yakovlevich | title=Continued Fractions | publisher = University of Chicago Press, Chicago and London | year = 1964}}</ref>

[[Aleksandr Korkin]] and [[Yegor Ivanovich Zolotaryov]] proved in 1873 that the first two [[Lagrange number]]s are the square root of 5 and the [[square root of 8]], which later inspired the work of [[Andrey Markov]] on what became known as [[Markov's theorem]].<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/Markov_s_Theorem_and_100_Years_of_the_Un/RXDGBAAAQBAJ|title=Markov's Theorem and 100 Years of the Uniqueness Conjecture: A Mathematical Journey from Irrational Numbers to Perfect Matchings|first=Martin|last=Aigner|date=July 18, 2013|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|via=Google Books| page=40}}</ref>

==Algebra==
The two [[quadratic field]]s {{tmath|\Q\bigl(\sqrt{5}~\!\bigr)}} and {{tmath|\Q\bigl(\sqrt{-5}~\!\bigr)}}, [[field extension]]s of the [[rational numbers]], and their associated rings of integers, {{tmath|\Z\bigl[\tfrac12 + \tfrac12\sqrt5~\!]}} and {{tmath|\Z\bigl[{\sqrt{-5} }~\!]}}, respectively, are basic examples and have been studied extensively.

The [[ring (mathematics)|ring]] <math>\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]</math> contains numbers of the form <math>a + b\sqrt{-5}</math>, where {{math|''a''}} and {{math|''b''}} are [[integer]]s and <math>\sqrt{-5}</math> is the [[imaginary number]] <math>i\sqrt{5}</math>. This ring is a frequently cited example of an [[integral domain]] that is not a [[unique factorization domain]].<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Chapman | first1 = Scott T.
 | last2 = Gotti | first2 = Felix
 | last3 = Gotti | first3 = Marly
 | editor1-last = Badawi | editor1-first = Ayman
 | editor2-last = Coykendall | editor2-first = Jim
 | contribution = How do elements really factor in <math>\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]</math>?
 | doi = 10.1007/978-981-13-7028-1_9
 | location = Singapore
 | mr = 3991169
 | quote = Most undergraduate level abstract algebra texts use <math>\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]</math> as an example of an integral domain which is not a unique factorization domain
 | pages = 171–195
 | publisher = Birkhäuser/Springer
 | series = Trends in Mathematics
 | title = Advances in Commutative Algebra: Dedicated to David F. Anderson
 | year = 2019| arxiv = 1711.10842
 | isbn = 978-981-13-7027-4
 | s2cid = 119142526
 }}</ref> For example, the number 6 has two inequivalent factorizations within this ring: <math>6 = 2 \cdot 3 = (1 - \sqrt{-5})(1 + \sqrt{-5}). \, </math>

On the other hand, the real [[Quadratic integer#Quadratic integer rings|quadratic integer]] ring of [[golden integers]] <math>\Z[\varphi]</math>, adjoining the [[golden ratio]] <math>\varphi = \tfrac12\bigl(1 + \sqrt{5}~\!\bigr)</math>, was shown to be [[Euclidean domain|Euclidean]], and hence a unique factorization domain, by Dedekind. This is the ring of integers in the [[golden field]] {{Q(√5)}}.<ref>{{citation |last=Dodd |first=Fred W. |year=1983 |title=Number theory in the quadratic field with golden section unit |place=Passaic, NJ |publisher=Polygonal Publishing House |isbn=0-936428-08-2 |url=https://archive.org/details/numbertheoryinqu0000dodd/ |url-access=limited}}</ref>

The [[field (mathematics)|field]] <math>\mathbb{Q}[\sqrt{-5}],</math> like any other [[quadratic field]], is an [[abelian extension]] of the rational numbers. The [[Kronecker–Weber theorem]] therefore guarantees that the square root of five can be written as a rational [[linear combination]] of [[roots of unity]]:
:<math>\sqrt5 = e^{2\pi i/5} - e^{4\pi i/5} - e^{6\pi i/5} + e^{8\pi i/5}. \, </math>{{Citation needed|date=July 2025}}

== Decimal calculation ==

As of January 2022, the numerical value in decimal of the square root of 5 has been computed to at least 2.25 trillion digits.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Yee |first1=Alexander |title=Records Set by y-cruncher |url=http://numberworld.org/y-cruncher/records.html}}</ref>
